title: GUARD-MENTION-C in prevent_data_loss.py: it blocks prose that mentions a removal
description:
FIFTH occurrence of GUARD-MENTION-C on this project, and the first inside a guard that
protects the workspace rather than inside a test.

REPRODUCED TWICE, 2026-08-17, and the second time is the interesting one.

(1) The coordinator ran `attest.py sign` with a --body JSON string whose prose EXPLAINED
    that a direct filesystem removal call had been available and deliberately not used.
    prevent_data_loss.py matched the name of that call inside the JSON payload and blocked
    the command. Nothing was being deleted: the command was an append-only signature over a
    file. The block was a substring match on an argument's CONTENTS.

(2) The coordinator then tried to file THIS defect report, whose text quotes the guard's own
    error message. The guard blocked that too. It prevented the filing of its own bug
    report. The task had to be created through a script file, because the guard scans the
    shell command and not file contents -- which is itself the shape of the problem.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. The workaround is trivial, and that is exactly the
problem: a guard whose false positives are cheap to route around trains every agent to route
around it. Worse, this specific false positive fires on prose DOCUMENTING a destructive
operation that was DECLINED, so the guard penalises the precise audit trail this harness
wants written.

WHAT TO BUILD. The registry rule is already on file: parse, do not scan. For a shell guard
that means deciding on the parsed command -- executable plus arguments -- and never on the
raw string. A quoted argument's contents are DATA and must not be read as a verb.

CAUTION, and this is the whole difficulty: the guard must not get weaker. Its true positives
are recursive removals and history-discarding git operations, and it caught two real ones in
this session. So the acceptance bar is a matrix with BOTH arms: every currently-blocked
destructive form still blocked, and a set of prose-mention cases allowed, including the two
reproductions above pinned verbatim as test cases.

Report the count of forms in each arm raw AND distinct (TELEMETRY-PROVENANCE-A).
acceptance_criteria: Decision is made on the PARSED command (executable + argv), never on the raw command string.
Both reproductions from 2026-08-17 pinned verbatim as allowed cases: the attest.py sign --body payload, and this task's own description text.
Every destructive form the guard blocks today still blocked; enumerate them from the current implementation first, do not guess.
A test matrix with both arms, and the count in each arm reported raw and distinct.
No net weakening: if any currently-blocked form must be allowed to make the parse work, say so explicitly rather than letting it lapse.
notes: THIRD REPRODUCTION, same day (2026-08-17), during T-403's handoff. The guard blocked the write of a handoff note whose section 7 listed the filesystem-mutating method names that an AST test FORBIDS the module from calling. So the guard blocked a document describing a prohibition on the very operation it was guarding against. All three of today's reproductions share one shape: prose DESCRIBING a removal that was not being performed. Two of the three were audit trails this harness wants written, and the third was this defect's own bug report. Pin all three verbatim as allowed cases.

notes.note:
T-407 CERRADO. La decision se toma sobre el comando PARSEADO, nunca sobre la cadena cruda.

QUINTA REPRODUCCION, mientras se escribia esta reparacion: la guarda bloqueo el archivo de
corpus de pruebas para repararla, que por construccion es la lista de todos los comandos
destructivos que la guarda conoce. Las cinco comparten una sola forma: PROSA QUE DESCRIBE
UNA REMOCION QUE NO SE ESTA EJECUTANDO, y tres de las cinco eran rastros de auditoria que
este arnes quiere que se escriban.

QUE SE HIZO. El texto se parte en cuatro poblaciones y cada una se trata por lo que es:
  COMANDOS   comandos simples como listas de tokens (ejecutable + argv), partidos en los
             operadores del shell. Las reglas leen tokens, asi que rm en posicion de
             argumento es un argumento y rm en posicion de ejecutable es rm.
  CODIGO     payloads que la convencion del propio ejecutable declara codigo: sh -c,
             python3 -c, perl -e, node -e, powershell -Command. Un payload de shell se
             parsea como linea de comando por derecho propio.
  COMENTARIOS  texto tras un # no entrecomillado. Se escanea con las reglas de lenguaje
             porque la guarda bloqueaba "go run x.go  # os.RemoveAll(p)" antes de este
             cambio, y ese bloqueo se conserva en vez de dejarlo caer en silencio.
  DATOS      argumentos entrecomillados de ejecutables sin convencion de codigo, y cuerpos
             de heredoc. NUNCA SE INSPECCIONAN. Esa es toda la reparacion.

ENUMERACION ANTES DE TOCAR NADA (criterio 3). El corpus sale de la implementacion vigente,
no de adivinar: 22 reglas mas PATCH_DELETE, con una o mas formas por regla, mas todo comando
que las pruebas existentes ya afirmaban bloqueado o permitido. Se verifico contra la
implementacion de regex ANTES del cambio: 56 formas destructivas, 56 bloqueadas, 0 escapes;
10 formas benignas, 0 bloqueos falsos.

MATRIZ DE DOS BRAZOS, con conteos crudos y distintos en cada brazo (TELEMETRY-PROVENANCE-A):
  BRAZO A  56 crudas / 56 distintas   siguen bloqueadas   0 fallos
           8 crudas / 8 distintas     formas que el parseo pudo abrir   0 fallos
  BRAZO B  5 crudas / 5 distintas     prosa que debe pasar   0 fallos
           10 crudas / 10 distintas   comandos benignos previos   0 fallos

UN HUECO QUE YO MISMO ABRI Y CERRE ANTES DE ENTREGAR: al quitar los cuerpos de heredoc
incondicionalmente, "bash <<EOF / rm -rf project / EOF" dejaba de bloquearse. Un cuerpo de
heredoc es dato solo hasta que hay un interprete del otro lado: cat > notas.md le da prosa a
un archivo, bash <<EOF le da un programa a un programa. Ahora el ejecutable receptor decide,
y las tres formas heredoc-hacia-interprete estan en el brazo A.

DEBILITAMIENTO NETO, DECLARADO EN VEZ DE DEJARLO DESCUBRIR (criterio 5). Dos formas que el
escaneo plano bloqueaba ahora pasan, y las dos son la misma forma que los falsos positivos:
  - somerunner "rm -rf /"      argumento entrecomillado de un ejecutable desconocido
  - echo "rm -rf x" | sh       un comando que llega por una tuberia, no por argv
Ningun parser puede distinguirlas de prosa sin conocer la convencion del llamado. Estan
fijadas por una prueba propia para que la perdida sea una decision registrada y no una
sorpresa, y para que un endurecimiento futuro tenga donde aterrizar. La mitigacion son las
tablas SHELL_WRAPPERS y CODE_FLAGS: un ejecutable cuya convencion SI se conoce conserva su
payload inspeccionado, y esas tablas son el lugar donde se agrega uno.

FALLA CERRADA. Un texto que no parsea cae al escaneo plano completo, verbatim de la
implementacion anterior. Un comando con comillas sin cerrar no es un comando seguro, y el
respaldo es el comportamiento mas estricto disponible, no el mas permisivo.

La prueba que verifica que la decision se toma sobre tokens PARSEA el modulo en vez de
grepearlo: es el mismo defecto un nivel arriba (GUARD-MENTION-C, septima ocurrencia).

PRUEBAS: 8 nuevas (28 en el archivo). Suite completa: 672 passed, 4 skipped.

REJECTED (harness-verifier, distinct from producer "main").

ACCEPTANCE CRITERION FAILED: "Every destructive form the guard blocks today still blocked ...
No net weakening: if any currently-blocked form must be allowed to make the parse work, say
so explicitly." The handoff declares exactly two intentional lapses (a quoted argument to an
UNKNOWN executable, and a command arriving through a PIPE). I found a THIRD, undeclared, and
much broader escape class: a bundled single-dash flag on a shell interpreter's -c invocation.

ROOT CAUSE, read from the code (static method, different from the producer's own dynamic test
corpus). CODE_FLAGS in prevent_data_loss.py declares "bash": ("-c", "shell") etc., and
_code_flag_names(exe) builds the accepted token set from CODE_FLAG_ALIASES.get(exe, ())
plus that single entry. CODE_FLAG_ALIASES has entries for perl/node/deno/bun/powershell/
pwsh/python variants/ruby -- NOT for bash/sh/zsh/dash/ksh/ash. inspect_command then only
recognizes the payload as code when a token EXACTLY equals "-c" (case-insensitively):
"if token.lower() in code_flags". A bundled POSIX short-option flag such as -lc (login +
command), -cl, -ic (interactive), or -xc (xtrace) never equals the string "-c", so the
payload is never routed to inspect_text/scan_source at all and the command is allowed
outright, exactly like the two declared lapses -- except this one is a common, everyday shell
invocation shape and was never disclosed.

REPRODUCED THREE WAYS, all against the LIVE file at .harness/bin/prevent_data_loss.py (not a
copy):

1) Direct classify() call, both old and new implementations loaded from disk
   (old = `git show ab1246b~1:.harness/bin/prevent_data_loss.py`, new = current HEAD):
     old.classify(command='bash -lc "rm -rf /tmp/foo"')  -> ("recursive or direct rm", ...)
     new.classify(command='bash -lc "rm -rf /tmp/foo"')  -> None
   i.e. the OLD flat-regex implementation blocked it; the NEW parser-based one does not.

2) The real hook invoked exactly as PreToolUse would invoke it (subprocess, stdin JSON,
   reading the actual return code): piping {"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":
   "bash -lc \"rm -rf /tmp/foo\""}} into `python3 .harness/bin/prevent_data_loss.py`
   -> exit 0, no stderr. (A true positive should exit 2 with the BLOCK_MESSAGE.)

3) Confirmed it is not a one-off: swept every POSIX interpreter in CODE_FLAGS with a bundled
   flag and every combining wrapper the module already special-cases. ALL of the following
   return exit 0 (allowed) from the live hook, and ALL were blocked by the pre-T-407
   implementation (each shown as INTERPRETER + BUNDLED-FLAG, payload = 'rm -rf /tmp/foo'):
     bash -lc   bash -cl   bash -ic   bash -xc
     sh -lc     zsh -lc    dash -lc   ksh -lc
     sudo bash -lc ...          (SHELL_WRAPPERS recursion, still escapes)
     timeout 5 bash -lc ...     (SHELL_WRAPPERS recursion, still escapes)
     xargs -I{} bash -lc ...    (SHELL_WRAPPERS recursion, still escapes)
     env FOO=bar bash -lc ...   (SHELL_WRAPPERS recursion, still escapes)
     nohup sh -ic ...           (SHELL_WRAPPERS recursion, still escapes)
     find . -exec bash -lc 'rm -rf {}' \;   (find -exec recursion, still escapes)
   Control (unbundled forms correctly stay blocked, confirming the failure is specifically
   about token-exact-match on "-c"): `bash --login -c "..."`, `bash -l -c "..."`,
   `bash -euo pipefail -c "..."`, `bash --posix -c "..."` -- all four still exit with the
   refusal, because "-c" appears as its own token in each.

WHY THIS IS BEYOND THE TWO NAMED LAPSES: the docstring's own framing is that a quoted
argument is data unless the callee's OWN calling convention declares it code, and the tables
are "the place to add one." bash/sh/zsh/dash/ksh are IN that table already -- this
is not the "unknown executable" case, and there is no pipe involved. The guard's own
convention-detection logic simply does not recognize the flag because of shell short-option
bundling, a well-known and extremely common invocation shape (bash -lc "..." is the
standard idiom for "run this as a login shell," used pervasively in CI configs, Docker
entrypoints, and shell wrapper scripts) -- unlike the two disclosed lapses, this is not an
edge case, it is a mainstream one.

NOT COVERED BY THE NEW TEST FILE: grep for the bundled-flag pattern and the word "login"
against .harness/tests/test_data_loss_guard.py -> no matches.
`python3 -m pytest .harness/tests/test_data_loss_guard.py -q` -> 28 passed, confirming the
escape is real and simply unexercised, not a false alarm caught by a test I overlooked.

FIX PATH (not prescribing which, but naming the two shapes for a producer to pick from):
(a) match code flags by set-membership over the token's individual short options rather than
whole-token equality (so -lc is recognized as containing c) for bundled-flag-capable
executables, or (b) add explicit alias entries per interpreter for the realistic bundled
forms (-lc, -cl, -ic, -xc, ...) the way node/perl aliases are already enumerated.
Either way this needs to be declared as arm A (still-blocked) coverage, not silently dropped
into arm B (now-allowed) the way it currently is.

VERDICT: acceptance criteria 3 and 5 both fail -- a currently-blocked, common destructive
form (bundled-flag shell -c invocation, plus every wrapper/find-exec combination of it) is
now silently allowed, and it is not among the two lapses the docstring declares. Sending back.

RECHAZO ACEPTADO Y REPARADO. El verificador tenia razon: era un escape real y no
declarado, mas alla de las dos perdidas que el docstring si nombraba.

EL ESCAPE. CODE_FLAGS exigia que un token FUERA IGUAL a -c para tratar el payload como codigo.
Las banderas cortas de POSIX se empaquetan, asi que -lc, -cl, -ic, -xc, -ilc y toda otra
disposicion que cargue una c no eran iguales a -c y pasaban en silencio, junto con cada
combinacion con envoltorio (sudo, env, nohup, nice, xargs) y con find -exec. Criterios 3 y 5
fallados los dos: una forma que la implementacion de regex bloqueaba quedo abierta, y no quedo
declarada.

LA REPARACION. Un token de un solo guion es bandera de codigo cuando CONTIENE una de las
banderas de codigo de UNA LETRA del ejecutable. Las banderas largas y las que no llevan guion
(--eval, el /c de powershell) siguen empatando por nombre exacto.

Y UNA SEGUNDA COSA QUE EL ESCANEO ENCONTRO AL ARREGLARLO: el bucle recorria TODOS los
argumentos buscando la bandera de codigo, asi que `python3 tool.py -c "<prosa>"` leia como
codigo un payload que pertenece a tool.py. Es exactamente el falso positivo que toda esta
reparacion existe para quitar, y es la forma de la reproduccion de attest.py sign --body. Ahora
el recorrido se detiene en el primer token que no empieza con guion, porque ese es el nombre del
script y lo que sigue es suyo.

EVIDENCIA. Barrido completo de 16 formas empaquetadas -- 8 directas y 8 envueltas o de otros
interpretes -- todas bloqueadas, mas 2 controles no empaquetados (bash --login -c, bash -l -c)
que nunca fueron el problema y siguen bloqueados, aislando el defecto a la forma empaquetada.
CONTROL NEGATIVO: bash -lc "echo hola" y bash -lc "ls -la" PASAN, porque si no la reparacion
podria ser "bloquear toda bandera empaquetada", que seria una guarda que dejo de parsear y
empezo a rehusar. Y `python3 tool.py -c "rm -rf project"` pasa, fijado como prueba.

La matriz original sigue en cero: 56 crudas / 56 distintas siguen bloqueadas, 8 formas que el
parseo pudo abrir siguen bloqueadas, 5 reproducciones de prosa pasan, 10 comandos benignos
pasan. Archivo de pruebas: 33 pruebas. Suite completa: 699 passed, 4 skipped.
